# Overview

In this tutorial, we will:

1. Simulate a small ERP dataset with a hierarchical study design
   (trials nested in stimuli/conditions, nested in participants).
2. Walk through the 9 steps to building an LME: from the maximal model,
   simplified until it converges, through checking assumptions and
   visualizing the results.
3. Interpret the final model's fixed and random effects, and see how
   centering and coding (dummy vs. effects) change what the coefficients mean.
4. Illustrate common issues with LMEs (non-convergence,
   mis-specified random effects, REML vs. ML comparisons) so you recognize
   these errors and know how to fix them in your own data.
5. Go through some more examples of centering predictors (grand-mean centering vs.           centering within cluster).

---

# Simulating an ERP Study

## Study design

Children aged 3–5 years view faces expressing two emotions ("happy" and "angry"), 
each expression displayed by several different actors, with each actor/emotion 
combination repeated across 10 trials (a fully-crossed design where every 
participant sees every actor express every emotion the same number of times).
Each child's age (in years) is a participant-level variable: one value per child.

```{r design-params}
# Study design parameters --------------------------------------------------
n_subjects       <- 40      # number of participants
n_actors         <- 5       # number of actors per emotion condition
n_presentations  <- 10      # number of times each actor/emotion is shown
emotion_labels   <- c("Happy", "Angry")

# Population-level parameters 
mean_amp_happy   <- -10     # population NC mean amplitude for Happy (microvolts)
mean_amp_angry   <- -12     # population NC mean amplitude for Angry (microvolts)
decay_per_trial  <- 0.5     # amplitude becomes *less* negative by this much per presentation (habituation)
age_effect       <- -2      # amplitude becomes *more* negative by this much per year of age, 
                            # averaged over emotions (older children have larger NCs)
emotion_age_int  <- 1.5     # the Happy - Angry difference grows by this much per year of age
                            # (0.5 µV at age 3, 2 µV at age 4, 3.5 µV at age 5)
subject_sd       <- 10      # SD of random intercepts across participants
actor_sd         <- 5       # SD of random intercepts across actors
trial_noise_sd   <- 8       # single-trial (residual) noise SD

set.seed(425)
```


## Building the trial-level dataset

We simulate one row per trial. We simulate random intercepts for each participant
and each actor (stimulus feature). In addition, we simulate additional trial-level
noise.

```{r simulate-data}
subject_ids <- sprintf("%02d", 1:n_subjects)
actor_ids   <- sprintf("%02d", 1:n_actors)

# Random effects: one random intercept per participant, one per actor
# Each participant also gets one age (years), drawn uniformly between 3 and 5
subject_re <- tibble(SubjectID = subject_ids,
                      subj_intercept = rnorm(n_subjects, mean = 0, sd = subject_sd),
                      AgeYears = round(runif(n_subjects, min = 3, max = 5), 1))

actor_re <- tibble(ActorID = actor_ids,
                    actor_intercept = rnorm(n_actors, mean = 0, sd = actor_sd))

# Full trial-level grid: every participant x every actor x every emotion x every presentation
sim_data <- expand_grid(
  SubjectID  = subject_ids,
  Emotion    = emotion_labels,
  ActorID    = actor_ids,
  PresentNum = 1:n_presentations
) %>%
  left_join(subject_re, by = "SubjectID") %>%
  left_join(actor_re, by = "ActorID") %>%
  mutate(
    emotion_effect = case_when(Emotion == "Happy" ~ mean_amp_happy, 
                               Emotion == "Angry" ~ mean_amp_angry),
    # amplitude habituates (becomes less negative) across repeated presentations;
    # centered on the middle presentation so the emotion_effect above stays
    # interpretable as the mean amplitude at an "average" presentation number
    decay_effect = decay_per_trial * (PresentNum - mean(1:n_presentations)),
    # older children have larger (more negative) amplitudes; centered on age 4
    age_shift = age_effect * (AgeYears - 4),
    # Emotion x Age interaction: the Happy - Angry difference grows with age
    # (half of the interaction added to Happy, half subtracted from Angry, so the
    # age effect averaged over emotions is still age_effect)
    emotion_age_shift = if_else(Emotion == "Happy", 0.5, -0.5) * emotion_age_int * (AgeYears - 4),
    trial_noise = rnorm(n(), mean = 0, sd = trial_noise_sd),
    MeanAmp = emotion_effect + decay_effect + age_shift + emotion_age_shift +
      subj_intercept + actor_intercept + trial_noise
  )

glimpse(sim_data)

# Remove columns used in data simulation
sim_data <- sim_data %>%
  select(SubjectID, Emotion, ActorID, PresentNum, AgeYears, MeanAmp)

```

# Descriptive Statistics & Data Visualization

Before hypothesis testing by fitting a model, we will look at our data to inform
our model (e.g., data distribution, outliers, linearity).

```{r data-plotting}
# Distribution of mean amplitude
ggplot(data = sim_data, aes(x = MeanAmp)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Mean amplitude (µV)", y = "Count", 
       title = "Histogram of mean amplitude")

# Distribution of mean amplitude (by actor)
ggplot(data = sim_data, aes(x = MeanAmp)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Mean amplitude (µV)", y = "Count", 
       title = "Histogram of mean amplitude by Actor (stimulus feature)") +
  facet_wrap(~ActorID) # +facet_wrap(~ActorID+Emotion)

# Summary statistics by actor/stimulus feature
sim_data %>%
  group_by(ActorID) %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(MeanAmp),
            sd = sd(MeanAmp),
            median = median(MeanAmp),
            min = min(MeanAmp),
            max = max(MeanAmp))

# Distribution of mean amplitude (by emotion)
ggplot(data = sim_data, aes(x = MeanAmp)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Mean amplitude (µV)", y = "Count", 
       title = "Histogram of mean amplitude by emotion (condition)") +
  facet_wrap(~Emotion)

# Linearity of predictors
ggplot(data = sim_data, aes(x = PresentNum, y = MeanAmp)) + 
  geom_jitter() + 
  geom_smooth(formula = y ~ x, method = "lm") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 1)) + 
  labs(x = "Presentation Number", y = "Mean amplitude (µV)",
       title = "Checking linearity between presentation number and mean amplitude") # + facet_wrap(~Emotion+Actor)

# Linearity of age (a participant-level predictor: plot one mean per child)
sim_data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, AgeYears) %>%
  summarize(MeanAmp = mean(MeanAmp), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = AgeYears, y = MeanAmp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(formula = y ~ x, method = "lm") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Child's mean amplitude (µV)",
       title = "Checking linearity between age and mean amplitude")


```

# Fitting an LME

We'll follow 9 steps to building an LME:

## Step 1: Define the research question(s)

1. Is there a difference in NC mean amplitude elicited by Happy vs. Angry faces?
2. Does the magnitude of the NC emotion difference change with age (3 to 5 years)?

## Step 2: List all relevant variables

- SubjectID
- Stimulus type (ActorID)
- Trial presentation number (PresentNum)
- Emotion condition (Emotion)
- Age in years (AgeYears)

## Step 3: Draw the study design schematic

```{r design-diagram, fig.height=5.5}
subj_nodes  <- tibble(label = c("Subject 01", "Subject 02", "Subject 03", "…",
                                paste("Subject", n_subjects)),
                      x = 1:5, y = 2)
actor_nodes <- tibble(label = paste("Actor", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_actors)),
                      x = seq(1, 5, length.out = n_actors), y = 1)
emotion_nodes <- expand_grid(actor_x = actor_nodes$x,
                             Emotion = emotion_labels) %>%
  mutate(x = actor_x + if_else(Emotion == "Happy", -0.22, 0.22), y = 0)
edges <- expand_grid(x = subj_nodes$x[subj_nodes$label != "…"],
                     xend = actor_nodes$x)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = 2, yend = 1),
               colour = "grey75") +
  geom_segment(data = emotion_nodes, aes(x = actor_x, xend = x, y = 1, yend = 0),
               colour = "grey45") +
  geom_label(data = filter(subj_nodes, label != "…"), aes(x, y, label = label),
             fill = "#9CAF88", colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(data = filter(subj_nodes, label == "…"), aes(x, y, label = label),
            size = 6) +
  geom_label(data = actor_nodes, aes(x, y, label = label),
             fill = "#3D6080", colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_label(data = emotion_nodes, aes(x, y, label = Emotion, fill = Emotion),
             colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Happy = "#D4A24C", Angry = "#B5573B"),
                    guide = "none") +
  annotate("label", x = 3, y = 1.5, fill = "white", size = 3.5,
           label = "every subject sees every actor") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = -0.35, size = 3.5, fontface = "italic",
           label = paste0("each emotion box = ", n_presentations,
                          " presentations per subject  →  ", n_subjects, " × ",
                          n_actors, " × 2 × ", n_presentations, " = ",
                          n_subjects * n_actors * 2 * n_presentations,
                          " trials")) +
  labs(title = "Subjects and actors are fully crossed") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.3)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```


## Step 4: Categorize variables by type (categorical, numeric) & level (trial vs. subject)

- SubjectID: factor/categorical, participant
- ActorID: factor/categorical, trial
- PresentNum: numeric/continuous, trial
- Emotion: factor/categorical, trial
- AgeYears: numeric/continuous, participant

## Step 5: Assign fixed and random effects

### Fixed effects

- Emotion
- Presentation Number
- Age
- Interaction between Emotion x age (research question 2)
- Interaction between Emotion x presentation number? We don't have a hypothesis
  about it, but habituation could differ by emotion, so we will include it as a
  covariate

### Random effects syntax
- Random intercept only: `(1 | grouping)`, e.g., `(1 | SubjectID)` gives each participant their own baseline mean amplitude
- Random intercept + random slope: `(predictor | grouping)` or `(1 + predictor | grouping)`, e.g., `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID)` gives each participant their own baseline *and* their own emotion effect
  - The predictor (left of `|`) must vary *within* each level of the grouping factor (right of `|`)
- Uncorrelated intercept + slope: `(1 + predictor || grouping)`, which estimates the same variances but fixes the intercept–slope correlation at 0 (only works as intended with numeric predictors, it's uncommon to use this unless there's good theoretical evidence)

### Possible random effects in our design

*SubjectID*

- `(1 | SubjectID)`: Do some participants have higher or lower mean amplitudes on average?
- `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID)`: Does the effect of emotion (Happy vs. Angry) differ across participants?
- `(1 + PresentNum | SubjectID)`: Does habituation (change in amplitude across presentations) differ across participants?
- `(1 + Emotion * PresentNum | SubjectID)`: Does the change in the emotion effect across presentations differ across participants?
- **No** `(1 + Age | SubjectID)`: each child has only one age, so age doesn't vary *within* a participant and an age slope by participant can't be estimated. Age is a fixed effect (a measured characteristic of each child), not a random effect.

*ActorID*

- `(1 | ActorID)`: Do some actors' faces produce larger or smaller mean amplitudes overall, across both emotions?
- `(1 + Emotion | ActorID)`: Does the effect of emotion differ across actors (e.g., some actors pose a more intense angry expression)?
- `(1 + PresentNum | ActorID)`: Does habituation differ across actors (e.g., amplitude drops faster for some faces)?
- `(1 + Emotion * PresentNum | ActorID)`: Does the change in the emotion effect across presentations differ across actors?
- `(1 + Age | ActorID)` and `(1 + Emotion * Age | ActorID)`: Does the age effect (or the way the emotion effect changes with age) differ across actors? Age varies within actors (each actor is seen by children of all ages), so these slopes *could* be estimated. But we have no theoretical reason to expect that some faces show larger age effects than others, so **we decided not to include them** in the maximal model. Decide this before you fit the model.

*SubjectID × ActorID (optional)*

- `(1 | SubjectID:ActorID)`: Do particular participants respond differently to particular actors, beyond the separate participant and actor effects? 

**Random slopes we'd prioritize:** a SubjectID × Emotion slope (Does the effect
of emotion differ across participants?) and an ActorID × Emotion slope (Does
the effect of emotion differ across actors?). These seem like the two most probable random effects we could observe and we also want to prioritize capturing variance in emotion condition. 

## Step 6: Consider data transformations & center predictors

*Data transformations (e.g., nonlinear effects):* There wasn't evidence for
nonlinear effects in our exploratory data visualization, so we would fit a linear effect of presentation number. 

*Centering presentation number:*
- Without an interaction (e.g., MeanAmp ~ Emotion + PresentNum + (1|SubjectID)), centering only effects the intercept.
- With an interaction (e.g., MeanAmp ~ Emotion*PresentNum + (1|SubjectID)), uncentered presentation number will give predicted amplitude for the reference emotion at trial 0 (a trial that doesn't exist in our numbering scheme, but you could re-number the trial numbers to create a real trial) at 0.
- Centering presentation number will give predicted amplitude for the reference emotion at the average trial.

*Centering age:* 
- Age is a participant-level predictor, so we could consider **grand-mean centering** (`Age_gmc` = age minus the sample's mean age). The intercept is then the predicted amplitude for a child of average age, instead of a child age 0.

*Naming conventions:* we label each centered variable by how it was centered: `_gmc` for grand-mean centered (e.g., `Age_gmc`, `PresentNum_gmc`) and `_cwc` for centered within cluster (e.g., `PresentNum_cwc`, later in the tutorial). 

*Coding Emotion:* for now, we'll use R's default **dummy coding**: Angry = 0 and Happy = 1, so Angry is the **reference group**. We'll come back to effects coding after we've fit and interpreted the final model (see "Circling back: dummy vs. effects coding").

```{r center-predictors}
sim_data <- sim_data %>%
  mutate(PresentNum_gmc = PresentNum - mean(PresentNum),
         PresentNum_True0 = (PresentNum - 1))

# Grand-mean center age using one value per child (the mean of the children's ages)
mean_age <- mean(distinct(sim_data, SubjectID, AgeYears)$AgeYears)
sim_data <- sim_data %>%
  mutate(Age_gmc = AgeYears - mean_age)

sim_data %>%
  select(SubjectID, Emotion, MeanAmp, PresentNum, PresentNum_gmc, PresentNum_True0,
         AgeYears, Age_gmc)
```


## Step 7: Fit the maximal model and simplify until convergence is reached

We'll start from our theoretically-driven maximal model and simplify it **one
random effect at a time**, using a "leave-one-out" approach: remove one random
effect, refit, and check the fit. If that doesn't fix the problem, put it back
and remove the matching random effect for the other grouping factor instead.
If neither version converges without a singular fit, remove both and move on
to the next type of random effect. We work through them in this order:

1. **Interaction slopes first (Step 7b):** they're the least plausible and the
   hardest to estimate.
2. **Then main-effect slopes (Step 7c):** presentation number (habituation)
   before emotion, because emotion is the effect we care most about. Within
   each pair, we try the ActorID slope first: with only `r n_actors` actors,
   there's the least information to estimate how actors differ.
3. **Until we reach random intercepts only (Step 7d),** or stop earlier as
   soon as a model converges without a singular fit.

At each step, we check:

- **Estimation warnings:** Is the fit singular or non-converging
  (`isSingular()`, `check_convergence()`)? This tells us *that* the model is
  too complex, but not *which* term is the problem.
- **Variance components:** In `VarCorr()` output, look for random-effect SDs
  near zero and correlations near ±1.

We'll use a helper function so each model prints the same diagnostics:

```{r check-fit-helper}
check_fit <- function(fit) {
  cat("Singular fit:", isSingular(fit), "\n\n")
  print(VarCorr(fit), comp = "Std.Dev.")  # random-effect SDs and correlations
}
```

### Step 7a: Fit the maximal model

```{r maximal-model, warning=TRUE}
# Maximal model following Barr et al. (2013)
fit_max <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion * PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) +  # children differ in amplitude, emotion effect, habituation,
                                                                  # and how the emotion effect changes over presentations
                  (1 + Emotion * PresentNum_True0 | ActorID),     # actors differ in amplitude, emotion effect, habituation,
                                                                  # and how the emotion effect changes over presentations
                data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_max)
```

A singular fit means the model estimated a random-effect variance at zero or a
correlation at ±1.

What the variance components tell us:

- **ActorID:** the slope SDs are close to zero, and several correlations are
  near ±1.
- **SubjectID:** the slopes are correlated with each other at about ±.99 or
  higher, so some terms are redundant with each other.

### Leave-one-out approach

Here's every model we would fit along the way to reaching a model that converges and doesn't have a singular fit. Some of these are in code chunks below to illustrate what the output looks like. 

**Round 1: interaction slopes** (starting from the maximal model, Step 7a)

- Remove the by-actor interaction slope:
  `(1 + Emotion * PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | ActorID)`
  → still singular (shown below as `fit_7b1`).
- Put it back and remove the by-participant interaction slope instead:
  `(1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion * PresentNum_True0 | ActorID)`
  → still singular, and it also fails to converge (not shown).
- Neither works, so remove both:
  `(1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | ActorID)`
  → still singular (shown below as `fit_7b2`).

**Round 2: presentation-number slopes** (habituation)

- Remove the by-actor slope (do actors differ in how fast children habituate to them?):
  `(1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion | ActorID)`
  → still singular (shown below as `fit_7c1`).
- Put it back and remove the by-participant slope (do children habituate at different rates?):
  `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | ActorID)`
  → still singular (not shown).
- Neither works, so remove both:
  `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion | ActorID)`
  → still singular (shown below as `fit_7c2`).

**Round 3: emotion slopes** (the effect we care most about, so these go last)

- Remove the by-actor slope (do actors pose emotions with different intensity?):
  `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID)`
  → still singular: the by-participant emotion slope is tiny, with a correlation of
  −1 with the intercept (shown below as `fit_7c3`).
- Put it back and remove the by-participant slope (do children differ in their emotion effect?):
  `(1 | SubjectID) + (1 + Emotion | ActorID)`
  → still singular: the by-actor emotion slope has a correlation of +1 with
  the intercept (not shown).
- Neither works, so remove both:
  `(1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID)`
  → converges and isn't singular: this is our final random-effects structure
  (Step 7d, `fit_int1`).

### Step 7b: Remove the interaction slopes

Round 1, first try: remove the ActorID interaction slope.

```{r model-7b1}
fit_7b1 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion * PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) +
                  (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | ActorID),
                data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_7b1)
```

Still singular. Removing only the SubjectID interaction slope instead is also
singular (not shown), so we remove both:

```{r model-7b2}
fit_7b2 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) +
                  (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | ActorID),
                data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_7b2)
```

Still singular, so we move on to the main-effect slopes.

### Step 7c: Remove the main-effect slopes

Round 2, first try: remove the ActorID presentation-number slope (different
habituation for different actors).

```{r model-7c1}
fit_7c1 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) +
                  (1 + Emotion | ActorID),
                data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_7c1)
```

Still singular. Removing only the SubjectID presentation-number slope instead
is also singular (not shown), so we remove both presentation-number slopes:

```{r model-7c2}
fit_7c2 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion | SubjectID) +
                  (1 + Emotion | ActorID),
                data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_7c2)
```

Still singular. Round 3, first try: remove the ActorID emotion slope
(different actors express the emotions with different intensity).

```{r model-7c3}
fit_7c3 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion | SubjectID) +
                  (1 | ActorID),
                data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_7c3)
```

Still singular: the by-participant emotion slope SD is only
`r round(attr(VarCorr(fit_7c3)$SubjectID, "stddev")[["EmotionHappy"]], 2)` µV
(next to an intercept SD of about 10 µV), and its correlation with the
intercept is at ±1. Removing only the by-participant emotion slope instead is also
singular (not shown), so we remove both emotion slopes.

### Step 7d: Random intercepts only

```{r model-random-intercept}
fit_int1 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                   (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                 data = sim_data)

check_fit(fit_int1)
performance::check_convergence(fit_int1)
```

This model converges and isn't singular, so this is our **final random-effects
structure**. That matches our simulation: we only simulated random intercepts,
so every slope's true SD is 0. Next we look at the fixed effects (Step 7e).

### Step 7e: Looking more at our fixed effects interactions (optional)

Once we've reached the maximal random effects structure that converges, we're going to look more at our fixed effects to demonstrate some possible decisions we may have made (e.g., about centering). We might also pre-register some model simplification steps about our fixed effects (e.g., if interactions don't significantly improve model fit, we will remove interactions to fit a more parisimonious model). Or we might compare competing models (e.g., we might fit two models that each have a different behavioral predictor that is correlated, e.g., including either income or education level attained, see example in Mon et al., 2024). 

The two interactions in our model:

- **Emotion × Age is research question 2, so we keep it** whatever the test
  shows. If a hypothesized interaction isn't significant, report it as
  non-significant (estimate, 95% CI, *p*). Dropping it because it wasn't
  significant is a data-driven choice that makes the remaining *p*-values look
  more certain than they are.
- **Emotion × Presentation number is a covariate.** We might pre-register that if this interaction doesn't improve model fit (likelihood-ratio   test, *p* > .05), we will omit it for a simpler model.

Nested models (models in which one is a simplified version of another) can be tested using the lme4::anova function. anova(fit_no_ep, fit_int1) runs a likelihood-ratio test (LRT): does the bigger model fit the data significantly better than the smaller one? It reports each model's AIC, BIC, log-likelihood and deviance, then a χ² test. The χ² is the difference in deviance, and its df is the number of extra parameters (here 1, for the interaction). A significant p means the extra term improves the fit. Because the models differ in their fixed effects, anova() automatically refits both with maximum likelihood (ML) instead of REML before comparing them (refit = TRUE, the default). To compare models that differ only in their random effects, add refit = FALSE to keep REML.


```{r fixed-effects-lrt}
# Without the Emotion x Presentation number interaction (same random effects)
fit_no_ep <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * Age_gmc + PresentNum_True0 +
                    (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                  data = sim_data)
anova(fit_no_ep, fit_int1)   # refits both with ML (REML = FALSE)
```

The Emotion × Presentation number interaction doesn't improve the fit
(*p* = `r round(anova(fit_no_ep, fit_int1)$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2], 2)`), so following our rule, we will remove it.
Emotion × Age stays in because it's one of our research questions.

Here's our **final model**, fit with REML (the default):

```{r final-model}
fit_final <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * Age_gmc + PresentNum_True0 +
                    (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                  data = sim_data)

summary(fit_final)
tab_model(fit_final)
```

### Describing the simplification in your methods

In a methods section, you might write: *"We began with the maximal
random-effects structure (Barr et al., 2013), without by-actor slopes for age,
which we had no theoretical reason to expect. We simplified it one term at a
time until the model converged without a singular fit, removing interaction
slopes first and then main-effect slopes, starting with the by-actor slopes and
keeping the by-participant emotion slope until last (Bates et al., 2015;
Matuschek et al., 2017). We then tested the emotion × presentation
number interaction, which we had pre-specified as a covariate, with a
likelihood-ratio test, and removed it because it did not improve model fit
(χ²(1) = `r sprintf("%.2f", anova(fit_no_ep, fit_int1)$Chisq[2])`, *p* =
`r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.2f", anova(fit_no_ep, fit_int1)$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2]))`). The final
model included random intercepts for participants and actors, and fixed
effects of emotion, presentation number, age (grand-mean centered), and the
emotion × age interaction."*

## Step 8: Check model assumptions

The assumptions of an LME are similar to those of linear regression
(Heise et al., 2022, Section 2.2):

1. **Linearity:** continuous predictors are linearly related to the outcome.
2. **Normal distribution of residuals:** the residuals follow a normal
   distribution and aren't skewed.
3. **Homoscedasticity (homogeneity of variance):** the residuals have similar
   spread across groups (e.g., emotion conditions) and across the range of
   predicted values.

Unlike linear regression, LME does **not** assume that data points are
independent, because the random effects model the dependence among trials
from the same participant or actor. LME does add one assumption of its own:
the random effects (e.g., each participant's intercept) are also assumed to be
normally distributed.

We check all of these at once with `check_model()` from the performance
package (Lüdecke et al., 2021), which draws one diagnostic plot per assumption.
It needs the **see** package installed to draw the plots.

```{r check-model, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}
check_model(fit_final)
```


What our plots show:

- **Influential observations:** the green contour lines labeled 0.8 mark the
  Cook's distance cutoff, and every point is inside them. A few points sit
  close to the lines at the top and bottom edges, but none is anywhere near
  influential: the largest Cook's distance is
  `r round(max(cooks.distance(fit_final)), 3)`, far below 0.8, and
  `check_outliers(fit_final)` finds no outliers. All leverage values are tiny
  and nearly identical (no single trial out of 4,000 carries much weight), and
  they stack up into one narrow band because the design is balanced. The
  labeled points are just the largest residuals; being labeled doesn't make
  them a problem. In smaller plots (e.g., on a slide), the contour lines can
  fall outside the plotted range, which also means every point is inside them.
- **Collinearity:** all VIFs are close to 1, because age and presentation
  number are centered and the design is balanced.
- **Normality of random effects:** with only `r n_actors` actors, the actor
  panel has only 5 points so hard to interpret this plot but we'll say it looks okay.

**Why plots instead of tests?** With `r nrow(sim_data)` trials, formal tests
(e.g., Shapiro-Wilk for normality or a test for heteroscedasticity) can be significant even when there are only small deviations from the assumption. Some researchers recommend Shapiro-Wilk for samples up to 5,000 but other researchers suggest that Shapiro-Wilk is too sensitive even lower (e.g., at 4,000 observations). Beyond 4,000-5,000 observations/total trials you should use visual inspection.

### Reporting

You might write: *"Model assumptions (linearity, homogeneity of variance,
normality of the residuals and random effects, collinearity, and influential
observations) were checked by visual inspection of diagnostic plots
(`check_model()` in the performance package; Lüdecke et al., 2021)."*


## Step 9: Interpret and visualize results

### Interpreting the model output

Let's start with the model output:
```{r fit-final-interpretation}
# There's the default R output from our model
summary(fit_final)

# Here's output from the sjPlot package
tab_model(fit_final)

```

### Fixed effects

`Emotion` is a character variable, so R uses alphabetical order and **Angry is
the reference level**. `EmotionHappy` is therefore the Happy − Angry
difference. Because our model includes an Emotion × Age interaction, the
`Emotion` and `Age_gmc` coefficients are *simple effects*: each is the effect
when the predictor it interacts with is 0. So the emotion effect is for a child
of average age (`Age_gmc` = 0, i.e., `r round(mean_age, 1)` years), and the age
effect is for **Angry** faces. Presentation number doesn't interact with
anything, so its slope applies to both emotions.

```{r fixef-true0}
b_raw <- fixef(fit_final)
```

- **(Intercept) = `r round(b_raw["(Intercept)"], 2)` µV:** predicted mean amplitude for
  **Angry** faces on the **first presentation** (`PresentNum_True0` = 0), for a
  child of average age.
- **EmotionHappy = `r round(b_raw["EmotionHappy"], 2)` µV:** Happy faces elicit a mean
  amplitude `r round(b_raw["EmotionHappy"], 2)` µV more positive than Angry faces **for a
  child of average age** (simulated: `r mean_amp_happy - mean_amp_angry` µV at age 4).
- **PresentNum_True0 = `r round(b_raw["PresentNum_True0"], 2)` µV:** for both emotions, mean
  amplitude becomes `r round(b_raw["PresentNum_True0"], 2)` µV more positive with each
  additional presentation (habituation; simulated: `r decay_per_trial` µV).
- **Age_gmc = `r round(b_raw["Age_gmc"], 2)` µV:** for **Angry** faces, the
  predicted change in mean amplitude for each additional year of age
  (simulated: `r age_effect - emotion_age_int / 2` µV per year for Angry faces;
  p = `r round(summary(fit_final)$coefficients["Age_gmc", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3)`).
  Look at its df (≈ `r round(summary(fit_final)$coefficients["Age_gmc", "df"])`)
  and SE: age is a participant-level predictor, so it's tested against differences
  *between children* (SD ≈ `r round(attr(VarCorr(fit_final)$SubjectID, "stddev"), 1)` µV)
  with only `r n_subjects` children, not against the `r format(nrow(sim_data), big.mark = ",")`
  trials. A 2-to-3 µV-per-year effect over a 2-year age range is small next to
  that, so the estimate can land far from the simulated value. Participant-level
  effects need enough *participants*; more trials don't help.
- **EmotionHappy:Age_gmc = `r round(b_raw["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc"], 2)` µV:** how much
  the age effect differs for Happy vs. Angry faces (Happy age effect =
  `r round(b_raw["Age_gmc"] + b_raw["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc"], 2)` µV per year).
  Equivalently, how much the Happy − Angry difference grows per year of age
  (simulated: `r emotion_age_int` µV;
  p `r ifelse(summary(fit_final)$coefficients["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc", "Pr(>|t|)"] < .001, "< .001", paste("=", round(summary(fit_final)$coefficients["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3)))`).
  Unlike `Age_gmc`, this is tested against trial-level variability (look at its
  df), because the emotion effect is measured within each child.

### Visualizing the results

I prefer plotting the LME model's
**estimated marginal means** (EMMs) for the fixed effects of interest, rather
than raw averages because when we report our models we're reporting the model estimates (not the raw averages). EMMs are the model's predicted mean amplitude for each
condition, averaged over (or set at the mean of) the other predictors, so they
use every trial and account for the random effects. When it's possible, it's nice to show subject averages or trial-level variability so that readers get a sense of the means and spread of the data. We'll make three plots:

1. EMMs across repeated presentations 
2. EMMs for each emotion 
3. EMMs across age, our participant-level predictor

Error bars and ribbons show **±1 standard error (SE)** of each EMM. 

```{r visualize-results}
# Same colors for each emotion in every plot
emotion_colors <- c(Angry = "#D55E00", Happy = "#0072B2")

# 1. Model-estimated mean amplitude for each emotion across presentations
emm_final <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ Emotion | PresentNum_True0,
                     at = list(PresentNum_True0 = 0:(n_presentations - 1)),
                     lmer.df = "asymptotic")   # > 3,000 trials: asymptotic df

as.data.frame(emm_final) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PresentNum_True0 + 1, y = emmean, color = Emotion, fill = Emotion)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = emmean - SE, ymax = emmean + SE), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:n_presentations) +
  scale_color_manual(values = emotion_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = emotion_colors) +
  labs(x = "Presentation number", y = "Model-estimated mean amplitude (µV)",
       title = "Model-estimated NC amplitude by emotion",
       subtitle = "Ribbons = ±1 SE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Estimated marginal means for each emotion.** These are at the average
presentation number and the average age. The gray lines show each child's
observed mean for context: the EMMs summarize the population, while the gray
lines show how much children vary around it.

```{r visualize-emmeans-emotion}
# 2. EMMs for each emotion (at the average presentation number and age)
emm_emotion <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ Emotion, lmer.df = "asymptotic")
emm_emotion

# Each child's observed mean for each emotion
child_means <- sim_data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, Emotion) %>%
  summarise(MeanAmp = mean(MeanAmp), .groups = "drop")

as.data.frame(emm_emotion) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Emotion, y = emmean, color = Emotion)) +
  geom_line(data = child_means, aes(y = MeanAmp, group = SubjectID),
            color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = child_means, aes(y = MeanAmp), color = "grey65", size = 1.2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = emmean - SE, ymax = emmean + SE), width = 0.12, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = emotion_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean amplitude (µV)",
       title = "Model-estimated NC amplitude by emotion",
       subtitle = "Colored points and error bars = EMMs ± 1 SE; gray = each child's observed mean") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Estimated marginal means across age.** Age is a participant-level predictor, so
each point is one child's observed mean (one per emotion), and the lines are
the model's estimates across the age range.

```{r visualize-emmeans-age}
# 3. EMMs across the observed age range (at the average presentation number)
age_grid <- seq(min(sim_data$Age_gmc), max(sim_data$Age_gmc), length.out = 25)
emm_age <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ Emotion | Age_gmc, at = list(Age_gmc = age_grid),
                   lmer.df = "asymptotic")

child_age_means <- sim_data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, AgeYears, Emotion) %>%
  summarise(MeanAmp = mean(MeanAmp), .groups = "drop")

as.data.frame(emm_age) %>%
  mutate(AgeYears = Age_gmc + mean_age) %>%            # back to years for the x-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = AgeYears, y = emmean, color = Emotion, fill = Emotion)) +
  geom_point(data = child_age_means, aes(y = MeanAmp), alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = emmean - SE, ymax = emmean + SE), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = emotion_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = emotion_colors) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Mean amplitude (µV)",
       title = "Model-estimated NC amplitude across age",
       subtitle = "Lines and ribbons = EMMs ± 1 SE; points = each child's observed mean") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The lines aren't parallel: the Happy − Angry difference is small in the
youngest children and grows with age. That's the Emotion × Age interaction. The
age ribbons are wide because age is tested against only 40 children (df = 38),
not ~4,000 trials.

**Two more figures for a paper:**

- **The grand-average waveform**, averaged across all children (with no
  casewise deletion), so readers can compare with earlier ERP studies. Our
  simulation only has mean amplitudes, so we can't plot it here.
- **Single-trial waveforms from an example participant**, to show variability in single-trial data (can also go in Supplement for publications).

---

# Going further with the final model

## Circling back: dummy vs. effects coding

In Step 6, we said we'd come back to how Emotion is coded. Now that we have a
final model, we can see what changes when we code it differently.

So far, `Emotion` has used R's default **dummy (treatment) coding**: Angry = 0,
Happy = 1. With dummy coding, every effect that interacts with emotion is that
effect **in the reference group**. Our model has an Emotion × Age interaction,
so the `Age_gmc` coefficient above is the age effect *for Angry faces only*.

If we want those effects **averaged across both emotions** (what most people
mean by a "main effect"), we can use **effects coding** instead. There are two
common versions:

- **±0.5:** Angry = −0.5, Happy = +0.5 (the two levels are 1 unit apart)
- **±1:** Angry = −1, Happy = +1 (the two levels are 2 units apart)

Here's our final model fit all three ways. Presentation number and age are
the same as before (0 = the first presentation; age centered), so coding is the
only difference.

```{r effects-coding}
# Effects coding: Angry = -0.5, Happy = +0.5
# Effects coding: Angry = -1,   Happy = +1
sim_data <- sim_data %>%
  mutate(Emotion_e  = ifelse(Emotion == "Happy", 0.5, -0.5),
         Emotion_e1 = ifelse(Emotion == "Happy", 1, -1))

# Dummy coding (Angry = 0, Happy = 1) is our final model, fit_final

fit_final_effects <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion_e * Age_gmc + PresentNum_True0 +
                            (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                          data = sim_data)

fit_final_effects1 <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion_e1 * Age_gmc + PresentNum_True0 +
                             (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                           data = sim_data)

# Same model, just reparameterized: the predictions are identical
all.equal(fitted(fit_final), fitted(fit_final_effects))
all.equal(fitted(fit_final), fitted(fit_final_effects1))
```

**Another way: `contrasts()`.** Instead of making a new numeric variable, you
can keep `Emotion` as a factor and change how R codes it:

```{r effects-coding-contrasts, eval = FALSE}
sim_data_c <- sim_data %>%
  mutate(Emotion = factor(Emotion, levels = c("Angry", "Happy")))
contrasts(sim_data_c$Emotion) <- c(-0.5, 0.5)   # Angry = -0.5, Happy = +0.5

lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * Age_gmc + PresentNum_True0 +
       (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
     data = sim_data_c)
```

This gives the same estimates as `fit_final_effects`; only the coefficient's
name changes (`Emotion1` instead of `Emotion_e`). Keeping a factor is handy for
predictors with 3+ levels, and `emmeans()` and plotting functions keep the
level names (Angry, Happy). Two cautions:

- R's built-in `contr.sum()` codes the **first** level as +1. With Angry
  first, that makes Angry = +1 and Happy = −1, so the Emotion coefficient flips
  sign (and is half the Happy − Angry difference). Setting the values yourself,
  as above, avoids this.
- The `||` shortcut for uncorrelated random effects only works with numeric
  predictors. If you need `(1 + Emotion_e || SubjectID)`, use the numeric
  version.

### The output for each model

```{r effects-coding-output}
# # Dummy coding: Angry = 0, Happy = 1
# summary(fit_final)
# 
# # Effects coding: Angry = -0.5, Happy = +0.5
# summary(fit_final_effects)
# 
# # Effects coding: Angry = -1, Happy = +1
# summary(fit_final_effects1)

# Side-by-side with sjPlot
tab_model(fit_final, fit_final_effects, fit_final_effects1,
          dv.labels = c("Dummy (Angry = 0, Happy = 1)",
                        "Effects (Angry = -0.5, Happy = +0.5)",
                        "Effects (Angry = -1, Happy = +1)"))
```

### All coefficients side by side

The three models name the emotion terms differently (`EmotionHappy`,
`Emotion_e`, `Emotion_e1`), so we line them up by what each term is:

```{r effects-coding-table}
# Pull the fixed effects from one model and label each term by its role
coef_by_role <- function(fit, emo, coding) {
  tidy(fit, effects = "fixed") %>%
    mutate(Term = case_when(
             term == "(Intercept)"                         ~ "Intercept",
             term == emo                                   ~ "Emotion",
             term == "PresentNum_True0"                 ~ "Presentation number",
             term == "Age_gmc"                               ~ "Age",
             term == paste0(emo, ":PresentNum_True0")   ~ "Emotion × Presentation number",
             term == paste0(emo, ":Age_gmc")                 ~ "Emotion × Age"),
           Coding = coding)
}

term_order <- c("Intercept", "Emotion", "Presentation number", "Age",
                "Emotion × Presentation number", "Emotion × Age")

# Line up the three codings of one model in a single table
coding_table <- function(fit_dummy, fit_e05, fit_e1) {
  coding_tab <- bind_rows(
      coef_by_role(fit_dummy, "EmotionHappy", "dummy"),
      coef_by_role(fit_e05,   "Emotion_e",    "e05"),
      coef_by_role(fit_e1,    "Emotion_e1",   "e1")) %>%
    transmute(Term = factor(Term, levels = term_order), Coding,
              b  = round(estimate, 3),
              SE = round(std.error, 3),
              t  = round(statistic, 2),
              p  = ifelse(p.value < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = Coding, values_from = c(b, SE, t, p),
                names_glue = "{Coding}_{.value}") %>%
    arrange(Term) %>%
    select(Term, starts_with("dummy_"), starts_with("e05_"), starts_with("e1_"))

  kable(coding_tab, col.names = c("Term", rep(c("b", "SE", "t", "p"), 3))) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1,
                       "Dummy (Angry = 0, Happy = 1)" = 4,
                       "Effects (Angry = -0.5, Happy = +0.5)" = 4,
                       "Effects (Angry = -1, Happy = +1)" = 4))
}

coding_table(fit_final, fit_final_effects, fit_final_effects1)

b_dum <- fixef(fit_final)
b_eff <- fixef(fit_final_effects)
b_ef1 <- fixef(fit_final_effects1)
```

### What changed and what didn't?

| Coefficient | Dummy (0/1) | Effects (±0.5) | Effects (±1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | Angry faces, first presentation, average age: `r round(b_dum["(Intercept)"], 2)` µV | Average of Happy and Angry: `r round(b_eff["(Intercept)"], 2)` µV | Same as ±0.5: `r round(b_ef1["(Intercept)"], 2)` µV |
| Emotion | Happy − Angry: `r round(b_dum["EmotionHappy"], 2)` µV | Happy − Angry: `r round(b_eff["Emotion_e"], 2)` µV | **Half** of Happy − Angry: `r round(b_ef1["Emotion_e1"], 2)` µV |
| Presentation number | Habituation (both emotions): `r round(b_dum["PresentNum_True0"], 3)` µV | Same: `r round(b_eff["PresentNum_True0"], 3)` µV | Same: `r round(b_ef1["PresentNum_True0"], 3)` µV |
| Age | Age effect for **Angry**: `r round(b_dum["Age_gmc"], 2)` µV | Age effect **averaged** over emotions: `r round(b_eff["Age_gmc"], 2)` µV | Same as ±0.5: `r round(b_ef1["Age_gmc"], 2)` µV |
| Emotion × Age | Happy age effect − Angry age effect: `r round(b_dum["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc"], 3)` | Same as dummy: `r round(b_eff["Emotion_e:Age_gmc"], 3)` | **Half** of that: `r round(b_ef1["Emotion_e1:Age_gmc"], 3)` |

**Dummy vs. effects coding changes the lower-order effects that interact
with emotion** (the intercept and age). The effects-coded age effect sits
halfway between the Angry and Happy age effects, so it equals the dummy-coded
(Angry) age effect + ½ × the Emotion × Age interaction:
`r round(b_dum["Age_gmc"], 2)` + ½ × `r round(b_dum["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc"], 2)` =
`r round(b_dum["Age_gmc"] + 0.5 * b_dum["EmotionHappy:Age_gmc"], 2)` µV. (We simulated
`r age_effect - emotion_age_int / 2` µV per year for Angry faces and `r age_effect`
µV per year averaged over emotions. With only `r n_subjects` children, age is
estimated imprecisely, so in another sample these estimates could land far from
the simulated values; see the fixed-effects interpretation above.) Its *p*-value changes too, because it's now
testing a different question (the average age effect instead of the Angry one).
Presentation number doesn't interact with emotion, so it's the same in all
three.

**±0.5 vs. ±1 only rescales the emotion terms.** Happy and Angry are 2 units
apart with ±1 coding, so the emotion coefficient (and every interaction with
emotion) is the change per unit, which is *half* the Happy − Angry difference.
The SEs are halved too, so the *t* and *p* values are identical to ±0.5. The
intercept and the presentation number and age effects don't change at all.

**Which age effect would you report?** With dummy coding, "the age effect" is
really the age effect for Angry faces, which is steeper than for Happy faces.
Reporting it as *the* age effect would overstate how much NC amplitude changes
with age in general. The effects-coded estimate is the average over both
emotions.

### Marginal means don't depend on coding

Instead of refitting with a different coding, you can keep the dummy-coded
`fit_final` and get the effects you want from **estimated marginal means**
(EMMs). `emmeans()` gives the model-estimated
Nc for each emotion, and `emtrends()` gives the age effect (slope) for each
emotion. These are predictions from the model, so they're the same no matter
how Emotion is coded.

```{r emmeans-coding}
# Model-estimated mean Nc for each emotion (at the average age and presentation number)
emm_coding <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ Emotion, lmer.df = "asymptotic")
emm_coding
pairs(emm_coding, reverse = TRUE)   # Happy - Angry

# Age effect (µV per year) for each emotion, and averaged over both
emt_coding <- emtrends(fit_final, ~ Emotion, var = "Age_gmc", lmer.df = "asymptotic")
emt_coding
emtrends(fit_final, ~ 1, var = "Age_gmc", lmer.df = "asymptotic")
```

- **Emotion:** at the average age and presentation number, Happy faces
  elicited a less negative Nc than Angry faces (Happy − Angry =
  `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(pairs(emm_coding, reverse = TRUE))$estimate)` µV).
- **Age:** the age effect is
  `r round(summary(emt_coding)$Age_gmc.trend[1], 2)` µV per year for Angry
  faces and `r round(summary(emt_coding)$Age_gmc.trend[2], 2)` µV per year for
  Happy faces, or
  `r round(summary(emtrends(fit_final, ~ 1, var = "Age_gmc", lmer.df = "asymptotic"))$Age_gmc.trend, 2)`
  µV per year averaged over both. These match the coefficients above:
  the dummy-coded `Age_gmc` is the Angry slope, and the effects-coded
  `Age_gmc` is the average.

## Centering

**Presentation number.** The intercept above is for the first presentation.
To get it at the **average** presentation instead, we re-fit the model with
`PresentNum_gmc` (presentation number minus its mean,
`r mean(sim_data$PresentNum)`):

```{r fit-final-centered}
fit_final_centered <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * Age_gmc + PresentNum_gmc +
                             (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                           data = sim_data)

# Side-by-side: first presentation = 0 vs. average presentation = 0
tab_model(fit_final, fit_final_centered,
          dv.labels = c("PresentNum_True0", "PresentNum_gmc"))

b_cen <- fixef(fit_final_centered)
```

Only the intercept changes (`r round(b_raw["(Intercept)"], 2)` →
`r round(b_cen["(Intercept)"], 2)` µV): presentation number doesn't interact
with anything, so the emotion effect, the age effect, and the interaction are
identical. This is what Step 6 said: without an interaction, centering only
changes the intercept.

**Age.** Age *does* interact with emotion, so where age = 0 sits changes the
meaning of the emotion effect. With raw age in years, `EmotionHappy` would be
the emotion effect at age 0, a newborn, far outside our 3-to-5-year-olds:

Without centering, the emotion coefficient (dummy coded) shows that Happy faces would be about 4 µV more negative than Angry faces in a newborn. That's the opposite direction of the +2.00 at the average age. 

```{r fit-final-raw-age}
fit_final_rawage <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * AgeYears + PresentNum_gmc +
                           (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                         data = sim_data)

bind_rows(`Age_gmc (0 = average age)` = tidy(fit_final_centered, effects = "fixed"),
          `AgeYears (0 = newborn)`   = tidy(fit_final_rawage, effects = "fixed"),
          .id = "Model") %>%
  filter(term == "EmotionHappy") %>%
  select(Model, estimate, std.error, statistic) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Model", "EmotionHappy (µV)", "SE", "t value")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

b_rawage <- fixef(fit_final_rawage)
```

## Standardized betas as an effect size

Raw coefficients are in different units (µV per presentation, µV per year), so
they're hard to compare with each other or across studies. **Standardized
betas** (β) put every effect in standard deviation (SD) units: the change in
amplitude, in SDs, for a 1-SD change in the predictor. To get them, we standardize every variable (including mean amplitude) with `scale()`
(subtract the mean, divide by the SD), name each one `_z`, and refit the final
model:

```{r standardized-betas}
# Age is a child-level variable: scale it with one value per child, so children
# with more trials don't count more toward the mean and SD
age_z <- sim_data %>%
  distinct(SubjectID, AgeYears) %>%
  mutate(Age_z = as.numeric(scale(AgeYears))) %>%
  select(SubjectID, Age_z)

# Trial-level variables: scale across all trials
sim_data_z <- sim_data %>%
  left_join(age_z, by = "SubjectID") %>%
  mutate(MeanAmp_z    = as.numeric(scale(MeanAmp)),
         PresentNum_z = as.numeric(scale(PresentNum)),
         Emotion_z    = as.numeric(scale(Emotion == "Happy")))   # balanced design, so Angry = -1, Happy = +1

# The final model, with standardized variables
fit_final_z <- lmer(MeanAmp_z ~ Emotion_z * Age_z + PresentNum_z +
                      (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                    data = sim_data_z)

# Standardized betas with 95% CIs
beta_tab <- tidy(fit_final_z, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")
beta_tab %>%
  transmute(Predictor = term,
            `β` = round(estimate, 3),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", conf.low, conf.high),
            p = ifelse(p.value < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

b_z <- setNames(beta_tab$estimate, beta_tab$term)
```

How to read them:

- **Presentation number, β = `r round(b_z["PresentNum_z"], 2)`:** for each 1-SD
  increase in presentation number (`r round(sd(sim_data$PresentNum), 1)`
  presentations), amplitude changes by `r round(b_z["PresentNum_z"], 2)` SDs.
- **Age, β = `r round(b_z["Age_z"], 2)`:** for each 1-SD increase in age
  (`r round(sd(distinct(sim_data, SubjectID, AgeYears)$AgeYears), 2)` years),
  amplitude changes by `r round(b_z["Age_z"], 2)` SDs.
- **Emotion, β = `r round(b_z["Emotion_z"], 2)`:** emotion is binary, so a
  "1-SD change" is less intuitive. With a balanced design, `Emotion_z` is −1
  for Angry and +1 for Happy (2 units apart), so the Happy − Angry difference
  is 2 × β = `r round(2 * b_z["Emotion_z"], 2)` SDs. If you'd rather report the
  full difference directly, keep emotion at ±0.5 and standardize only the
  outcome and the continuous predictors.

### Checking the emotion effect with emmeans

Three ways to get the Happy − Angry difference in SD units should all agree:

1. **2 × β** from the fully standardized model (`Emotion_z` = −1 / +1).
2. **The coefficient** from a model with emotion kept at **±0.5** (only the
   outcome and the continuous predictors standardized). Angry and Happy are 1
   unit apart, so no transformation is needed.
3. **The pairwise comparison** of the estimated marginal means (EMMs) from the
   raw model (in µV), divided by the SD of mean amplitude.

```{r emmeans-standardized}
# 2. Emotion at +/-0.5; outcome, age, and presentation number standardized
fit_final_z05 <- lmer(MeanAmp_z ~ Emotion_e * Age_z + PresentNum_z +
                        (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | ActorID),
                      data = sim_data_z)

# EMMs at Angry (-0.5) and Happy (+0.5), for average age and presentation number
emm_z05 <- emmeans(fit_final_z05, ~ Emotion_e, at = list(Emotion_e = c(-0.5, 0.5)),
                   lmer.df = "asymptotic")
emm_z05
pairs(emm_z05, reverse = TRUE)   # Happy - Angry, in SDs of amplitude

# 3. The same comparison on the raw model, in µV
emm_raw <- emmeans(fit_final, ~ Emotion, lmer.df = "asymptotic")
emm_raw
diff_raw <- pairs(emm_raw, reverse = TRUE)   # Happy - Angry, in µV
diff_raw

# All three, side by side
tibble(Method = c("2 × β (Emotion_z = −1 / +1)",
                  "Coefficient (Emotion = ±0.5, outcome standardized)",
                  "EMM difference in µV ÷ SD of mean amplitude"),
       `Happy − Angry (SD units)` = round(c(2 * fixef(fit_final_z)[["Emotion_z"]],
                                            fixef(fit_final_z05)[["Emotion_e"]],
                                            summary(diff_raw)$estimate / sd(sim_data$MeanAmp)), 3)) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

All three give the same Happy − Angry difference,
`r round(fixef(fit_final_z05)[["Emotion_e"]], 2)` SDs: Happy faces elicited
an Nc `r round(fixef(fit_final_z05)[["Emotion_e"]], 2)` SDs less negative than
Angry faces (for a child of average age). The EMMs and their pairwise
comparison work on the raw model too, which is often the easiest way to report
a condition difference: in µV (`r round(summary(diff_raw)$estimate, 2)` µV)
and, if you need it, in SD units.

A few things to keep in mind:

- **The t and p values don't change.** Standardizing only rescales each
  variable, so the tests are the same as in the unstandardized model.
- **The "SD" is the total SD of amplitude**, which includes differences
  between children and actors, not just trial-to-trial noise. Standardized
  betas from an LME aren't directly comparable to Cohen's *d* from a *t*-test
  on averaged data.
- **Report both**: unstandardized b (in µV, which ERP readers can picture) and
  standardized β (to compare effects and studies).


## Reporting in APA style

**My recommendation:** put every fixed effect in a **table** (maybe in Supplement), and in the text
report *b*, *SE*, *p*, and β for the effects you discuss.

The table below uses the effects-coded final model (`fit_final_effects`), so
each term is averaged over emotions, and the standardized β's from
`fit_final_z` in the section above.

```{r apa-table}
# APA formatting helpers: 2 decimals with a real minus sign; p with 3 decimals and no leading zero
f2 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
fp <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))

raw_tab <- tidy(fit_final_effects, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE)   # b, SE, 95% CI, t, df, p
std_tab <- tidy(fit_final_z, effects = "fixed")                          # beta (same term order)

apa_tab <- raw_tab %>%
  mutate(beta = std_tab$estimate) %>%
  transmute(Predictor = c("Intercept", "Emotion (Happy − Angry)", "Age (years, centered)",
                          "Presentation number", "Emotion × Age"),
            b = f2(estimate),
            SE = f2(std.error),
            `95% CI` = paste0("[", f2(conf.low), ", ", f2(conf.high), "]"),
            t = f2(statistic),
            df = ifelse(abs(df - round(df)) < .005, sprintf("%.0f", df), sprintf("%.2f", df)),
            p = fp(p.value),
            `β` = ifelse(term == "(Intercept)", "", f2(beta)))

apa_tab %>%
  kable(caption = "Fixed effects of the final model (effects coding: Angry = −0.5, Happy = +0.5)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

age_raw <- filter(raw_tab, term == "Age_gmc")
age_std <- filter(std_tab, term == "Age_z")
```

**In the text**, for the age effect:

> Averaged over emotions, age `r ifelse(age_raw$p.value < .05, "was", "was not")` significantly associated with Nc amplitude,
> *b* = `r f2(age_raw$estimate)`, *SE* = `r f2(age_raw$std.error)`,
> *p* = `r fp(age_raw$p.value)`, β = `r f2(age_std$estimate)` (see Table 1).


## Random effects

- σ2 = residual variance (trial-level variability)
- τ00 = random intercept variance (how much baseline amplitude differs by participant/actor)
- Variance is SD-squared, so taking the sqrt of variance estimates gives you SD (easier to interpret)
- e.g., variance of ~100 for subjectID means that sqrt(100) is equal to SD = 10 (participants' amplitudes differ from the overall intercept by ~10 microV)
- ICC = intraclass correlation coefficient (proportion of total variance due to differences between subjects + actors = ~66%)

These random-effect estimates are identical for `fit_final` and
`fit_final_centered`: centering a fixed-effect predictor doesn't change the
random intercept variances when the model has no random slopes.

If we're interested in what variance is attributed to participant variability vs. actor variability we can run:
```{r icc}
icc(fit_final, by_group = T)
```

---

# Common errors

## Error 1: Misspecifying the random-effects grouping structure

A subtler error: treating a within-subjects/crossed factor as if it were a
simple grouping factor, or vice versa. For example, `Emotion` in our design
is **crossed** with participants (everyone sees both emotions) — it should
never appear as a *grouping* variable like `(1 | Emotion)`, only inside the
random-effects term as a variable that's allowed to have a random *slope*
(e.g. `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID)`). Writing `(1 | Emotion)` fits a model
that treats "Happy" and "Angry" as if they were two random draws from a
larger population of possible emotions — nonsensical here, since we
deliberately chose these two conditions:

```{r fit-error-grouping}
fit_wrong_grouping <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ PresentNum + Age_gmc + (1 | SubjectID) + (1 | Emotion),
                            data = sim_data, REML = TRUE)
summary(fit_wrong_grouping)
```

Notice `Emotion` now has only 2 levels in its random-effect variance
component — R will fit this without erroring, which is exactly what makes
it dangerous. **A grouping factor with fewer than ~5 levels should almost
never be modeled as a random effect** (Volpert-Esmond et al., 2021);
instead it belongs as a *fixed* effect, as in our final model (`fit_final`). Always
sanity-check `summary(fit)$ngrps` or `VarCorr(fit)` to confirm the number
of levels going into each random-effect grouping factor matches what you
intended.

```{r check-ngrps}
summary(fit_final)$ngrps
```


## Error 2: Splitting one grouping factor across random-effects terms

It's tempting to write each random slope in its own set of parentheses, e.g.
`(1 + Emotion | SubjectID) + (1 + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID)`. But each set
of parentheses includes its own `1`, so this fits **two separate random
intercepts** for SubjectID, which the model can't tell apart. It splits the
participant intercept variance across the two terms (`SubjectID` and
`SubjectID.1` below) and is itself a cause of singular fits:

```{r duplicate-intercepts, warning=TRUE}
fit_dup <- lmer(MeanAmp ~ Emotion * PresentNum_True0 + Emotion * Age_gmc +
                  (1 + Emotion | SubjectID) + (1 + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID) +
                  (1 | ActorID),
                data = sim_data)
check_fit(fit_dup)
```

Put all slopes for a grouping factor in one term:
`(1 + Emotion + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID)`. If you want a slope *without*
its own intercept, use `0 +`, e.g. `(1 + Emotion | SubjectID) + (0 + PresentNum_True0 | SubjectID)`.
